definition.text: The state in which greenhouse gas emissions from human activity are balanced by human removals; often shortened to net zero.

facts.text: Reaching net zero is needed to slow global warming, though gases already in the air keep causing some warming.
It needs deep emission cuts first; a small remaining share can then be balanced by carbon dioxide removal.
Net zero standards require cutting emissions by more than 90% and offsetting only the remaining 10% or less.
The idea grew from late-2000s research showing warming slows only when CO2 emissions reach net zero, and it underlies the Paris Agreement.
As of November 2023 about 145 countries had announced or were considering net zero targets, covering close to 90% of global emissions.
The IMF estimates that net zero by 2050 would leave global GDP 7 percent higher than current policies.
Net zero, carbon neutrality and climate neutrality are often used as synonyms, but some standards give them different meanings.

definition.text: Residual emissions are those not practical to cut for technical reasons; robust net zero rules say they must be balanced by removals that store carbon as long as the gas would last.

facts.text: Methane lasts around 12 years in the air, carbon dioxide between 300 and 1,000 years, so removals balancing CO2 must last much longer.
Avoided-emissions offsets cut emissions against a baseline but remove nothing from the air; weaker carbon neutrality standards allow them.
Critics worry offsets delay real emission cuts and aid greenwashing.

definition.text: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol's division of an organisation's emissions into direct emissions, purchased energy, and its wider value chain.

facts.text: Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources a company owns or controls, such as its fuel and vehicles.
Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat, cooling or steam.
Scope 3 covers suppliers and product users; it made up 75% of emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project.
Oil companies claiming net-zero operations leave out customers burning their oil, 70–90% of oil-related emissions, which falls in Scope 3.

definition.text: The point that short-lived gases such as methane need not reach zero to halt warming, because cutting them lowers their warming effect at once.

facts.text: Net zero for CO2 alone can be reached sooner than for all greenhouse gases, partly because farm methane is harder to phase out.
Short-lived gases still push temperatures up in the short term and could breach 1.5 °C earlier.
Robust net zero standards cover all greenhouse gases, not only CO2.

title: Credibility of net-zero pledges

definition.text: The debate over whether net-zero targets are trustworthy, given that most are voluntary and lack enforcement.

facts.text: As of 2023 only 5% of companies with a net zero commitment had a credible plan, and credible targets covered only 7% of emissions.
Heavy reliance on carbon credits is a main reason many claims lack credibility.
The UN has condemned fossil fuel companies' net zero pledges, made while expanding production, as greenwashing.
Some climate scientists argue net zero lets actors put off cuts today by relying on unproven future technologies.

contested_note: Scientists and the UN question many net zero pledges, while standards bodies try to make them robust.

definition.text: A major structural change in how energy is supplied and used; today, the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy.

facts.text: The current transition aims to cut energy emissions mainly by phasing down fossil fuels and running as much as possible on low-carbon electricity.
Energy production and use cause most human greenhouse gas emissions, and fossil fuels meet over three-quarters of energy needs.
An earlier transition took place in the Industrial Revolution, from wood and biomass to coal, then oil and gas.
The term arose after the 1973 oil crisis and was popularised by Jimmy Carter in 1977.
Falling solar and wind costs have driven the transition since the late 2010s.
Despite decades of climate policy, transitions have not sped up beyond historical trends and remain off track for climate targets.

title: Energy additions
article: Energy transition#Examples of past energy transitions

definition.text: The view that humanity has never truly switched energy sources but has kept adding new ones on top of old ones.

facts.text: One school, described by Vaclav Smil, sees successive transitions in the shares of the energy mix: biomass, coal, oil, then a mix.
Jean-Baptiste Fressoz's school notes that 19th-century coal did not replace wood; more wood was burned too.
As of 2024, use of all forms of primary energy had increased, leading some to call 'transition' a slogan.

contested_note: Historians disagree whether past energy changes were transitions or additions.

title: Falling cost of renewables
article: Energy transition#Cost competitiveness of renewable energies

definition.text: The steep drop in the cost of wind, solar and batteries that has made them the cheapest new power in many regions.

facts.text: From 2010 to 2019 unit costs fell 85% for solar, 55% for wind and 85% for lithium-ion batteries.
Onshore wind or solar with a few hours of storage already has lower levelized cost than gas peaking plants.
In 2021 renewables made up more than 80% of new electricity generating capacity.

title: Critical minerals for the energy transition

definition.text: Minerals needed for clean energy technologies, whose demand is set to rise steeply with the transition.

facts.text: The IEA lists 37 critical minerals and expects demand for them to rise 235 per cent by 2050.
For mineral-rich countries of Sub-Saharan Africa the transition may drive sustainable development.
Mining for these minerals can threaten conservation areas and contributed strongly to deforestation in 2023.

definition.text: How shifting energy sources changes the relations, dependencies and fortunes of countries and companies.

facts.text: Owners of fossil or renewable resources face big losses or gains depending on how the transition unfolds.
The transition is expected to reduce reliance on long-distance fossil fuel trade and raise the role of regional markets.
Energy security became a stronger driver in Europe after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

definition.text: The aim that communities gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and take part in decisions about it.

facts.text: It has procedural, distributive and recognition dimensions.
Distributive justice concerns how energy revenues, infrastructure sites and costs are shared; cities often gain while rural areas bear burdens.
Procedural justice requires transparent decisions and meaningful consultation.
Transitions may worsen energy insecurity for low-income households.

definition.text: The goal of meeting all energy use from renewable resources.

facts.text: It is motivated by emissions, pollution, and economic and energy security concerns.
Research on it is fairly new, with few studies before 2009.
